Cod yesterday when the weather be-
came threatening and Captain Bly, de-
cided to run into Providencetown. Be-
fore he reached the end of the cape
the vessel ran on to the Peaked Hill
bar. Captain BLY, burned his signal
torch and then ordered his crew into
the boats. Four of the men jumped
into a dory, which was almost i'm
mediately capsized. Captain Bly, and
four others left the vessel a few min
utes later. Before the rest of the
crew could follow their skipper the
wind and sea had driven the Fish
Hawk over the bar and she was navi-
gated into Providencetown harbor.

CHARLESTON W. Va, Dec. 15-While
crowded with people. including many chill
dren on the way to school, the old sus-
pension bridge which connects East and
West Charleston collapsed today, turning
turtle as 1t fell. throwing twenty to thirty

hfty feet below The ice broke under the

ously. the United States engineers being

nal injuries; Lille Cavendar, sixteen, bruls-

SANTA ROSA, Feb. 24.-Mrs. T. L.
Neely and her daughter, Mrs. Eva
Kruse, received painful burns Tuesday
evening while cleaning pair of gloves.
Mrs. Neely was using gasoline and the
daughter put the gloves on her hands
to allow them to dry. Just as she had
pulled the gloves on. an oil stove began
making trouble, and the woman went
to attend it with the gasoline saturated
gloves on her hands. Evidently she
came too near the fire and her hands
were soon ablaze. In attempting to put
out the fire Mrs. Nicely also burned her
hands. Her dress caught fire and be-
fore it could be extinguished she had
been painfully burned about the nos
trils, upper lip and chin. The hands
of Mrs. Kruse were frightfully burned,
as the tight lifting gloves were thor
oughly soaked with the fluid, and she


has suffered terribly from the injuries.

Raymond r. Ecouly correspondent of the
Paris Temps at Liao-yang. has telegraphed
as follows to his paper:


II was fortunate this morning to travel
with an American naval attache. Lieut..
Newton McCully, who has just returned
from Port Arthur after a sojourn there of
three months. The news he gives me is en-
tirely different from the pessimisfic reports
received lately concerning the situation at
the fortress -,.- ~ -. ,.is.


The American attache left the fortress
August IA. The Japanese were then four
and a half miles from the city. The Rus
sian positions, upon chain of rugged hills
200 meters high, were projected by trenches.
mines. networks. barbed wire and cannon,
and. according to the American officer. it
was impossible to take them by assault.
Japanese shells fell in the city, but each po-
sition possessed dugout in which the oc-
cupants were able to secure shelter. The
Japanese heavy guns ceased firing every
night. fearing that the Russians would de-
tect their exact location by the flashes dur
ing the darkness.


There were considerable stocks of pro-
visions at Port Arthur. The Russian SOL
diers had a fresh-meat ration daily. The
reports that Russian officers were subsist-
ing on onions and black bread were absurd
inventions The stores were still open, and
the population promenaded the streets.


THE regiments took turns in the trenches.
Part of the garrison was always resting.
The Russian sailors assisted in the defense
of the fortress. They made excellent sharp
shooters. The heat had not been unbear-
able The American attache believes that
the Japanese losses have been very heavy,
at least ten times those of the Russians. In
short. Port Arthur can nold out much long
er than people believe.


When the officer left Port Arthur the
French naval attache, Lieut.. de Cuverville,
was still there. Entering and leaving the
fortress was then very difficult, as the
Japanese were sinking all the junks.


THE American officer landed at Shan
haikuan with some French women and one
little girl"

TUNA, Thibet, April 2.-The Thibetan
general, the whole of his personal escort
and five high Lhassa officials were among
the hundreds killed in the fighting of March
81 at Guru, Thibet


The small British losses are accounted for
by the fact that the Thibetans were so hud-
died together that the majority were unable
either to use their swords or to fire.


The swordsmen in the front rank could
not reach the Sikhs, who had fixed bayo-
nets, while the men IN the middle of the
mob could not reach the enemy, but many
of them probably killed each other in the
Tuad excitement.


The scene recalled old-time fights in cock
pits, the grim, determined faces of the Tki-
betans lighted with devildom, savagery, ex-
pressing contempt for the SlkhS, whom they
outnumbered six or seven TO one.


When the Lhassa general fired the first
shot the Thibetans, with wild shouts, drew
their swords, fired their matchlocks and
surged forward.


About dozen swordsmen made a desper-
ate rush in the direction of Colonel Macdon-
aid and a small knot of officers.


Four Thibetans attacked Mr. Gambler, the
correspondent of the London Daily Mail
but Colonel Macdonald seized a rifle and
shot two of them at few yards, and an
other officer killed the other two thus saw
ing Mr.. Gamblers life.


Those of the Thibetans who tried to climb
the wall were met with a terrible magazine
rifle fire, but they did not falter those behind
springing over the heaps of dead and con-
t!nuing the fight until riddled with bullets
When finally the Thibetans retired they
tramped back slowly and steadily, though
followed by a hail of bullets. A mountain
battery was brought into action and tore
the retreating lines with shrapnel A ter
rible trail of dead and dying marked the
line of march. At length the last wounded
limping Thibetan turned the corner some
four hundred yards from the scene of the
grim tragedy, where the best of the Thibe-
tan army had periShed.

ern Colorado and Northwestern Texas.

buildings in the town Of Florence were
badly damaged.


Telephone poles from Colorado
Springs clear to the southern line were
blown over, incapacitating the long

damage was done in other places along
the eastern slope of the mountains.
No less Of life or serious injury to per-
sons has been reported.

SALINAS, March 10.-The heavy wind
storm from the southwest hit Salinas
Valley about midnight last night and
continued until this forenoon. Since
then showers have fallen at intervals
The past twenty-four hours will show
that an inch of rain has fallen around
Salinas. Reports from the lower por-
tions of Monterey County indicate the
precipitation was heavier there Up to
noon to-day San Lucas had more
than an inch of rain, with prospects
for much more. Around Monterey and
along the coast the downpour has been
much heavier and was accompanied by
a fierce gale that uprooted trees and
blew down fences and outbuildings.


With the present storm has disap-
peared all fears of a poor season.
Throughout the Salinas Valley and
especially toward the San Luis Obispo
line the precipitation of the past month
has been far above. the average The
clear warm weather of the past two
weeks has caused a wonderful growth
in vegetation. The feed on the hills
around San Lucas, San Ardo, Bradley
and the cattle and sheep sections never





with young green grass and feed is
abundant.


In the Salinas Valley farmers who
have lived here for forty years predict
a record breaking season. While the
acreage may not be as large as usual
owing to the lateness of the season.
cereals Of every sort are growing with
wonderful rapidity. The soil has not
lost a bit of the rains and the warm
weather and lack of wind has quick
ened growth. From King City north to
the mouth of the Salinas River there
will be an unusually large beet acreage.
AS late rains are most needed in beet
raising, the prospects could not be bet
ter. While the seasons rainfall is below
the average, Monterey County pros
poets In all branches of agriculture
never looked better. The late rains and
warm weather have benefited crops in
all sections of the county. The lower
portion of the county has received a
plentitude of rain, and a general pros
perity is assured for the coming season

Another bad street car accident at

narrowly averted last night by the
presence of mind Of the motorman.


An Oak and Kenwood car had just
started downtown and was waiting at

watchman in the tower raised the
gates as the rear Of the train pulled
by and the conductor, who was new

coming from the opposite direction.

was but few rods from the crossing.
He quickly reversed and backed the
car, which missed being struck by
about two feet.


Passengers on the car say the
Waterman raised the gates before the

whelming Japanese force at bay when rife

years old She jumped from the narrow
coping at the fourth floor of the building

which she died this morning about $50
o'clock.


Mrs. Summers was employed at the Epis-

and some days ago she was brought to
washington and operated upon The opera
ton was successful and the patient seemed
to be Going well yesterday morning. Her
condition had been serious and her husband
remained here to await developments. Yes
terday morning he called at the hospital and
remained with his wife about two hours.
The patient appeared so much improved
that he returned to his place Of employment
In Virginia about noon.


About o'clock in the afternoon Miss Fee
ley, the nurse, had occasion to leave the
room for short time and upon her return
was surprised To find the bed without an
occupant and the window open.


Walking on Coping.


Looking out the window she saw the sick
woman walking along the narrow coping
from where fall. she realized, would mean
almost certain death. Without calling to
the coiored woman to return Miss Feeley
climbed upon the coping and went to the
rescue OF the woman, whose mind was ap-
parently impaired to a slight degree by
reason Of her sickness The nurse hardly
realized the perilous position in which she
had placed herself bur others who saw her
were made nervous by her daring conduct


Onlookers turned their heads for fear
there would be an awful tragedy enacted
when The women met. Miss Feeley walked
the narrow coping for more than fifty feet
and was not far from Mrs. Summers when
the latter either lost her balance or threw
herself from the building 1t was after this
was done that the nurse fully realized her
position and was able to return to the open
window without falling. The injured pa

hospital Despite the heavy fall she had ex-

She had sustained no broken bones but her

that the doctors felt satisfied that her life

notified. AS death had resulted from other
than natural causes the coroner had to be
notified Coroner hewitt visited the hospital
today end made an investigation. He saw
Miss Feeiey and had her explain how she had
climbed upon the coping and tried to save
the life of the patient. Mrs. Summers death,
the corcEer concluded, was due to an acct

EDEN, Colo, Aug. S.-w. Vance,
porter on the forward sleeping-car
Wyiuta. was one of the heroes of the
disaster. To him and his nerve and
bravery the people on that car owe
their lives.


Vance was standing near tha front
end of the car when the crash came
and with rare presence of mind rushed
to the hand brake on the front of the
car and began Tightening the brakes
on the wheels. His car was slipping
fol ward from the momentum and
from the terrible drag in front caused
by the forward cars falling into the
stream.


Vance held on to The brake like
grim death His hands clenched the
wheel until his fingers almost bled,
but he held on until his tight grip
stopped the car. The forward cars
broke from the sleeper and fell into
the water, while the car which Vance
had held with the brake stopped one
third Of the way on the brink of the
chasm, overhanging the gulch below
The forward trucks had left the track
and gone down, but the remainder of
the coach stayed on the tracks and
the lives of the passengers were saved


1t required two engines and nearly
a half hours work to pull this sleeper
back from the brink of the chasm.
Nothing but Vance's cool and brave
work at the brakes kept the car from
plunging into the stream.

While the Japanese have not been regard
| ed as having an especially efficient secret
| service. the events of the war have shown


that the persons who are watching day and
| night for them have been of the greatest
| value. 1t is known that just about the
| time the war broke out there were in Port
Arthur several French dancers who had
! c; red every Russian official heart Thoy
were not only attractive dancers but beau
| tiful women. who dressed well and had
nest engaging manners. The Russian
| officers were charmed with them. They
soon became better acquainted and proved
to be very agreeable companions They
took great interest in things military,
but always made amazing blunders in at
tempting to repeat what had been told
them. The womanly ignorance of such
matters charmed the young officers all the
i.tore, ana at the same time put them OFT
their guard But, a matter of fact,
they We're very clever women, and their
information was forwarded speedily to the
Japanese legation at Picking, which, In turn
forwarded valuable reports to Tokyo. by
the time their true character was known
the French actresses. who were spies Tor
the japanese, had left Port Arthur far be-
hind.


One of the most valuable assistants the
Japanese had at Port Arthur was a lttlo
servant who was not in the pay OF the
government. and who was not in any sense
attached to their secret service. In fact,
she was one of those poor little unknown
patriots who feel when their country Is at
war that they should give their own littlo
Insignificant aid.


A short time after the first lombard


ment the trains leaving Port Arthur wero
filled with refugees. The Japanese, of
course, thought 1t polite to make a change
of base, and the Russians were of the same
opinion. Many left Immediately, but the


little japanese servant remained. One
evening there was council and the sery-
ant, who was looked upon as an ignorant
little child, waited on the officers as usual
Plans and documents were spread upon the


table, the officers smoked, drank and dis
cussed the situation. The council lasted
late and then broke up. Finally there were


only a few remaining in the room. and
these, overtaken by lack of rest, fell asleep
The little waitress came into the room
again. saw the few officers remaining wero
asleep, quickly picked up bundle Of the


papers she saw lying on the table and


thrust them into the folds of her kimono


She had not the slightest idea of their i'm


portance what they were but the off,
GERS had been in such earnest discussion


that she gained the impression that they


would be useful to her government. Tho


first train out of Port Arthur that morning


had among its passengers the little serv-


ant who had disguised herself as n coolie


Before the-train started the papers had


been missed. and a file of soldiers was


drawn up alongside of the waiting cars.


while an inspector made a hasty search


among tHe passengers. he uld not, now


ever, detect the coolie, who never WINGED


during the search. The girl had been fa-


vorite with the officers, and had been


pected only when 1t was learned she had


left. The search proving unavailing the


train moved off toward Peking.


Arriving at Picking, the strengthening


little figure presented herself before the
door of the Japanese legation. function
airy tried politely to send her OFF, but she


persisted She must see the minister


But his excellency is engaged. Could


not the honorable gentleman call again?"


The matter was very important. How
important his excellepcy might know.


Finally the little spy was admitted. She
told the whole story. Matters of great i'm
portance indeed, were learned, and the
"coolie, replacing the strange mannish at
tire by the graceful kimono. received
sum of money and was sent to Japan.
There her achievement was loudly herald
ed and in her native town she soon became
the center of curiosity and admiration.

CHEFU, Sept. 13.-Port Arthur's g
semi-oficial journal, the Novi Krai. OF
date September announces that Cen
eral Stoessel, commander Of the fort
ress, has received a telegram Of con-
graduation from General Kuropatkin.
Early on the morning Of September a
thanksgiving service was held in the
barracks Of the Tenth Regiment on ac-
count of the Car having issued the
order that each month spent by the
troops in Port Arthur should count as
years service.


Operations are at present confined on
both sides to reconnoissanceS. All along
the line there are occasional encounters
between small detachments. The Novi
Krai gives many details of this desul-
tory fighting, showing that the Rus
slams are in the habit Of making recon
noissances that at times penetrate well
within the lines of the Japanese out
posts. These expeditions have devel-
oped the information that the Japanese
are constructing elaborate earthworks,
particularly at the east center of the
defense line.


On September three large merchant
men were sighted in Louisa Bay, and
many wagon trains were noticed NOV
ing to and from the bay. On the night
Of September the sea front port lights
revealed three Japanese torpedoboats
maneuvering close to the forts.


The Novi Krai remarks upon the
great energy Of the Japanese, who con-
tinue the work Of strengthening their
forts near Rihlungshan night and day.


On September some Russian scouts
stealthily approached the Japanese
lines and kidnapped five japanese SEN
tinels. Later they inadvertently ran
into some wires hung with bells, which
the Japanese had strung UP In order to
sound an alarm. When the bells began
ringing the Russians charged forward
firing the while. A Japanese detach-
ment in a trench returned the fire wild
ly for a moment and then retreated
The Russians gained the trench and
found forty-six Japanese dead there.


Two junks arrived here to-day from
Port Arthur One contained villagers
from Polantsu, which has been de-
stroyed. and the other brought 1S7 Chi
nese deported by the Russian authori-
ties. They reported that a junk carry
ing three Russian officers had been
captured by the japanese and taken
into Port Dalny.


The villagers of Polantsu complain
that It is the practice of the Russians
TO commander everything obtainabIe
in the way of eatables. They say the
soldiers often entered their houses and
took meals which had just been cooked
for themselves.


having difficulty with the powder they
manufacture at Port Arthur. A shell
fired from Golden Hill recently failed
to carry the proper distance and
dropped among some Russian troops

| There are several explanations OF the
| origin of the song 'Dixie's Land"
Everybody knows the name of the jolly
| comedian. Dan Emmett, who immortalzed
the ballad. but few know where he got the
phrase. One theory. long since exploded.
was that the expression pixies Land

| line. The other was that a certain farmer
down in New Jersey. just before the war.
| ran his fields with negro labor, and assumed

planter. His name was Dixie, and topical
songs of the period referred to his estate
as a miniature southland. Audiences which
did not know the local reference took the
song referring to the real south. and
Emmett. in his famous ballad, 50 used the
However, there Is another story, and one
which brings the subject home to New Or
leans. For twenty years prior to the civil
war the Citizens Bank OF Louisiana was
the great financial institution of the south.
and ranked among the one or two largest
in the land. Its name was as familiar upon


the Paris bourse and the London exchanges


as is now the name Of the City National


Bank of New York. In the days Of shin


plaSters' and deprecated state bank cur
rency the issues of the Citizens Bank pass
ed at par all over the land


The beSt-known issued a $40 note.
done in red upon one side and black and
red upon the other The feature Of this de-
nomination was that the most conspicuous
part of the engraving was the French word


DIX" Upon the river steamers, the
ships bound for New York. on the stage
coaches which went west from Galveston.
these bills were termed "Dixies." Not one
man of any twenty that handled them knew
that dix meant ten.


Upon the upper Mississippi and the Ohio
people began to speak Of the south
Dixie's Land. and as the years passed they
forgot why the name was applied. The
gamblers who won luscious rolls of the


'Dixies'' at poker played with the roof re-
moved. the victims who gave up their right
full walletfuls of red and black currency,
the Irish deckhands and the negro rOust-
abouts-aH spoke of Dixie's Land


The civil war came on. Months passed,
and Buffers army occupied the city. But
Ter ordered the Citizens Bank to pay back
all deposits to private individuals In con-
federate bills. and ordered that all sums
due to officers representatives OF the con-
federacy should be paid to the United States
government in United States coin. More
than $225 900 was thus confiscated and the
bank has now pending In Congress a war
claim for this amount. Later Gen. Butler
made the Citizens Bank the United States
depository and distributing center for the
territory under his charge.


After the war came new banking laws,
new customs, new ways and habits OF
thought The "Dixies'' had gone out during
the changes inaugurated Immediately be-
fore the civil war. and by the end OF that
struggle and the national banking law Of
the late Cos the once-famed currency was
forgotten

The first English walnut orchard in Cali
fornia was planted with seed from the Los
Angeles Mission gardens, where the padres
had started a few trees with nuts brought
with them from Spain. The undertaking
was a success from the first, and the acre
age of walnuts has steadily increased
slowly at first, but now with rapid strides.
The walnut trees early age Of bearing, its
long life and the steady demand for its
product tend to make the enterprise de-
servedly popular Already 1T Is suppressed
ing the orange in favor among fruit grow
ers.


The walnut tree begins to bear when six
or seven years old, and nothing Is known
definitely of it's age limit of bearing. Fabu-
lous stories told of trees in Spain one
or two centuries DID, bearing enormous
crops. The oldest trees in California are
still bearing. but deductions from the short
history already made show that the tree is
in it's prime from it's twenty-fifth to its thir-
tieth year. Fifteen hundred pounds of nuts
to the acre is good average yield, making
seventy-hve pounds the average weight
from one tree.


The harvest time begins about the middle
of September and lasts nearly six weeks
The nuts begin to fall with the leaves, and
the perfect cultivation under the trees
leaves no Nchance for them to lose them
selves among clods weeds. The brown
dead leaves alone hide the nuts. Under
normal conditions they drop free from the
outer husk. or hull, through it's irregular
bursting and getting the nuts picked up is
a simple matter. Sometimes the trees are
well irrigated just before harvest time to
insure the clean dropping of the nuts


Boys and girls, men and women, japanese
and Chinese, are all pressed into service.
and on hands and knees the great orchards
are gone over, not once, but several times
on account of the irregular ripening of tn
nuts. The trees are occasionally shaken
during the season to loosen the nuts, ana
before the last cleaning they are ''poled' to
start the very tardy ones This is done by
long, coarse, bamboo poles, whose light
weight makes them easily handled.


In certain rural districts the public
schools close regularly for a walnut vaca-
ton" The help of the children is needed.
and the children are nothing loath to re
plenfsh their diminished purses Pals, cans
and Aunnysacks are scattered among the
pickeVs and when the bags are full they
are carried to the drying grounds. where
they are spread out on slat trays to dry.

SANTA BARBARA, July 29-Making
her way down the Santa Barbara chan
mel as easily as a pleasure craft in the
shore breeze. the battleship Ohio, one
of the largest and most formidable
fighting vessels of the new navy, which
is to have her trial trip off this coast,
proceeded to her anchorage in the har-
Dor shortly before 10 o'clock this morn
ing. The Ohio had an easy trip from
San Francisco, and the $4,000 tons OF
steel and armament were propelled
down the coast and to her anchorage
place at the rate of twelve knots an
hour. 1t was expected the Ohio would
arrive in port at o'clock this morning


but as she sailed under slow speed
during the night in order to permit the
inspection of beaconS and to view the
land monuments after daybreak, the
trip was leisurely made.


Rear Admiral Whiting, representing
the United States Government, and
Chief Engineer Forsythe, representing
the Union Iron Works, expressed them
selves as being satisfied with all the ar
rangements and preparations made for
the official trip which will take place
Monday morning, weather conditions
permitting The trial trip will be over
a straightaway course, thirty-six miles
and return, the Government requiring
that an average speed of eighteen
nautical miles be made for the first two
miles each way. A ten-mile run will be
made in order that the Ohio may be
under full speed when the first stake
boat is passed. Chief Engineer For
sythe expressed entire confidence that
the Ohio would probably exceed the re-
quired speed by full knot, basing his
judgment upon the recent performance
of the battleship near San Francisco.
If this proves true the Ohio will exceed
the record of vessels of her class.


On board the Ohio are nearly 800 men
in the employ Of the builders and these
have been engaged throughout the day
giving the massive machinery general
overhauling and cleaning. The boats
that will attend the Ohio during the
trial trip are the gunboat Annapolis,
the torpedo-boat destroyers Perry, Paul
Jones and Preble and the Government
tugs Fortune and Unadilla. The Ohio
carries full armament of sixteen six
inch, twelve three-inch, six nine-pound-
| er and four Colt automatic guns.

text:
Summer dwellers who are accus


toned to believe that all the wonders
of the world are included within the
boundaries of Greater New York
will find in the huge new shaft lead
ing down to the Pennsylvania Rail-
road tunnel under the Hudson a sub
terranean wonder rivaling the Nam
moth Cave or the underground mys-
teries of Luray Cavern. This shaft,
says the New York Tribune, sunk at
the OUTER edge of the Tenderloin, at
Eleventh avenue and Thirty y-second
street, descends for 65 feet through
solid rock, and at this level forms the
point of departure for the twin tun-
nels under the Hudson.


To the visitor who peers nervously
over the mouth of this great opening,
60 feet long and 40 broad, and sees
faint lights flashing below or hears
confused murmurs of underground
activity, this pit seems to resemble an
entrance to Plutonian regions rather
than the commonplace creation of en-
gineers, planned to furnish an en-
trance to the new tunnel. To the
more daring, who tempt fortune by
descending the narrow wooden steps
that lead vaguely down into the damp
darkness below, the experience is
worth the semblance of danger Incl
dent to making it. Halfway down
the stairway turns, and here is the
boundary between the upper and
lower world. At this point the
mouth of the shaft, framing narrow
picture of cloud-hecked sky, resem-
b!es strikingly the open dome of the
Pantheon of Rome beyond and be-
meath the journey is made in ever-in-
creasing darkness.


But at the foot of the shaft imagi-
nation and sentiment end here the
visitor meets the practical and sees
the hand of the engineer. Straight
before him as he reaches the bottom
level are two ragged arches, hewn in
solid stone, and through them two
narrow gauge tracks vanish into
darkness carrying tiny cars laden
with rock blasted 200 feet beyond,
for the work has already marched
this far toward the Jersey shore.
These rough arches, smoothed and
lined, will one day make the passage
way for the great tubes. Already
the engineers are at work preparing
to equip the shaft with elevators,
and within short time material and
workmen alike will be lowered and
raised, and the wooden steps will lose
their usefulness.


Straight across the river, not more
than a mile away, is another shaft,
identical in general character with
that at Eleventh avenue and Thirty
second street. On that side of the
river also the two tubes have been
started, and for few feet the work
has gone under the solid rock.
dreds of workmen, who VIII gradu-
ally join those already at work, will
breathe. Through them also will
be raised, by elevators, soon to be put
in, all the stone blasted out OF the
tunnels. Some months later the
workmen, descending through these
shafts, one in Manhattan, one in
Weehawken, will meet far under the
Hudson, and then the tunnels will be
completed.

Gladstone Mich, Oct. 4.-Southern Alger
county adyices report desperate battle with
wolves to have been the thrilling experience Of
James Bosworth, civil veteran and home
steader. BoswOrth went in search of a COW, at
shutdown finding himself in big swamp, several
miles from home. He observed several wolves
making their way toward him, but, having his
rifle with him, he not alarmed. until he dis
covered that his ammunition was limited to one
cartridge.


Bosworth blazed away but. tho one of the


animals tumbled over, the others did not falter.
Then the homesteader realized the danger of
his situation. Quickly CHANGING about, he saw
that the wolves between him and small


beech with spreading branches, the only tree
near by which he could climb. Grasping his
rifle firmly, Bosworth awaited the attack, and,
swapping and snarling, the wolves leaped at him.
Using his gun as a club, BOsWOrth slowly made
his way toward the tree. AS wolf would
spring at him, he would fell 1t with a terrific
blow, only to receive attack. Sometimes
a wolf would succeed in reaching him, but finally
the veteran arrived at the foot of the tree,
where he shouted and charged toward the snarl
ing animals.


This momentarily disconnected them and gave
him sufficient respite to drop his gun and spring
| into the low-spreading branches, from which he
soon reached place of safety. The wolves
howled about the tree for some hours, and kept
Bosworth a prisoner until we'll into the night
when they disappeared suddenly as they
came.


AT daybreak the farmer made his way home
suffering from many painful but not serious
wounds Later in the day the pelt of the wolf
killed secured and the homesteader has
since collected the bounty the state and county
allow 1t is seldom that northern Michigan
| wolves will attack man. even. in winter, wher

The launch Mercedes of the United States
army quartermaster' department had a
narrow escape from sinking in her berth
at the harbor office wharf this morning
When the little craft was laid up for the
winter pine plugs were driven into the
openings in her sides where the pipes from
her pumps went overheard and the pipes
were disconnected. While she was working
with the tides in the ice this morning she
pulled out one Of the plugs. and through
the opening the water poured into her hull.


Fortunately, Capt. James Carpenter. who
has the launch in charge, made an inspec-
ton of the boat about that time. He found
her half full of water and sinking fast
With pumps and buckets. and aided by the
harbor force and the crews Of the tug Glib
bon ana yacht vafcour the water was
taken out of the boat and the hole in her
side closed before she was damaged.


The Mercedes is the tender to the War
Department, and Is used by the officers for
short trips on the river during the warm
weather. She Is a relic OF the war with
SPAIN having been one Of the tenders of
the Spanish cruiser Mercedes. and was cap
tured on that ship

A dispatch from Baltimore. last night
SAYS: Albert Ambuster late tonight shot
and seriously wounded Mrs. Dora Hoffman,
his mother-in-law, tried to kill his young
wife and then put bullet through his own
brain He will die, but his mother-in-law,
though seriously wounded, may recover.
His wife ESCAPED.


The attempted murder and the suicide
are the sequel to a suit for divorce brought
by Mrs Ambuster, who is only twenty-one
years old. They were married three years
ago She charged him with unfaithful-
ness The court yesterday granted her all
mony pending decision in the case. When
Ambuster broke into the house tonight his
wife was disrobed in her room bending over
their year-old babe in the crib. When the
Infatuated man burst into the room he fired
at his wife She ran, screaming. into her
mothers apartment. adjoining This room
was dark. Mrs. Hoffman was lying on
couch. As Ambuster entered she arose,
and. probably installing her for his wife,
he fred two shots at her. both infiicting
serious wounds He then fired again at
his wife. and rushing back into the room
where the baby lay, he fired his last bull
let into his own head and fell unconscious
beside the childs crib.

Big Basin Park.


SAN JOSE, Sept. s.-Nina Davenport
and Enid and Ettie Mckinney of this
city, who were guests in the Big Basin
Park when the destructive fire now
raging there started, returned to their
homes yesterday afternoon. They had
a thrilling experience in escaping from
the park, as they did not leave until
their camping place was almost sur
rounded by fire.


With Mrs. Hill and Miss Gertrude
Shelton of Petaluma, the young ladies
had been spending their vacation at
Governors Camp since August 15 At
2 o'clock Tuesday morning the party
of ladies received the first warning of
their danger. At that time they were
aroused by people residing at Union
Mill Tavern, who had come over to tell
the Warden that the forest all around
the basin was in flames The fire
burned very swiftly and by O'Clock
Wednesday afternoon was rapidly ap-
preaching the camp, despite the efforts
of the fifty men who were fighting IL
Thursday morning at Z o'clock Warden
Pilkington returned and told the ladies
to pack up what things they absolutely
needed and be prepared to leave. as
every moment lessened their chance of
escape.


At noon yesterday a party of eight
lumbermen from Blooms mill came
into Governors Camp and said that ali
avenues of escape had been cut off
with the exception of the trail by the
mill and the Pescadero trail. The
Misses Kinney, Miss Davenport. Mrs
HILL Miss Shelton and Mrs PiIkineton
at once started with their escort of
eight men. From Governors Camp the
distance is one and three quarter miles
to the mill and this distance the
women walked through the ashes and
sparks and almost suffocating smoke.


A rest was had at Blooms mill and
then the ladies walked nine miles to
Boulder Creek, from which place thew
came to San Jose by train


The Misses Kinney and Miss Daven-
port believe that they escaped from the
burning forests of the basin none too
soon.

commencement of this struggle the Russian
volunteer merchant fleet carried 5000
freight consignments from Poland to east
ern Asia during the year 1903, and the Rus
sian railroads and transportation COM
panies, in order to strengthen this export
trade against foreign competitors, chiefly
Americans and Japanese, had reduced the
regular freight rates and otherwise
sisted in the maintenance of this trade. But
the war with Japan has unsettled trade in
Manchuria, and the ground thus gained has
been entirely lost

Henry Pratt and Robert Hewlett, men,
bers of Capt. Boardman's corps of detec-
t.ves. spent several days in the woods near
Fredericksburg not long ago with dogs
and guns. When they started from here
they were certain they would have the
best sport of the kind they had ever en-
joyed. A delegation Of detectives escorted
them to the train and carried their outfit
for them They carried with them a big
stock of ammunition and were prepared TO
ship home their game III order that their
friends might enjoy wild turkey or some
fat birds or rabbits for their Thanksgiving
dinners.


But" said one Of the sportsmen upon
his return. "the dogs were almost worth
less and we also had other troubles


Their friends who had made preparations
for a feast were disappointed, although
they met the gunners upon their return
1t is unnecessary to state that their bag
sage could be handled with much less diff
Guilty than when they started for the VIZ
ginia fields. The first day on the fields put
the dogs out Of commission. The briars
were so thick and high that the CANNES
were scratched and cut and 1t appeared
that the city sports would have to abandon
their trip. They went out without dogs,
however, and got birds and rabbits enough
for a dinner.


The farmer at whose house they stopped
accompanied them to where they expected
to get their birds. and they had been out
but a short time before word came that
the farmers house was burning.


"And we left our overcoats in It," re-
marked one of the pair.


Hurryng back to the place where they
had slept the night before the city visitors
found two brick chimneys and a pile of
ashes to mark the site of the house.


1T guess our overcoats are gone" one OF
the detectives remarked to his companion.
And mine was a new one." added the
other.


The detectives had just reached the con-
clusion that they would charge up their
loss to the expense account for their out
Ing when Detective Pratt spied his garment
where 1t had been brought out with the
bedding. This recovery had reduced the
expense account several dollars. and search
was then made for the other coat. No
trace of the second coat was to be found
and the gunners had started to look for
another stopping place when they met a
woman carrying a child Wrapped about
the child was the coat that had caused the
men some little concern. Then the prob
lem resolved itself into a question as TO
whether the child or the owner of the coat
should wear the garment. and the child
won. Later the child was made comfort
able in a neighbours house and the men
came home much better off than they had
anticipated when they saw what the fire
had done.

BELGRADE, Servia, September 21.-Peter
Karageorgovitch was crowned King of
Servia today. There were no hostile demon
strations and no attempt to carry out the
numerous threats against the new king s
life. In the solemn ritual of the Greek
Church and in the elaborate state procession
which preceded and followed the corona
ton the tragedy of Servia's previous ruler
found no echo. Amid the thunder of the
saluting guns from the royal palace and
the garrison King Alexander's murder was
at least outwardly forgotten.


Brilliant Procession.


Here and in every garrison town of Servia
the dawn of day was marked by a salute of
twenty-one guns. and before the sun was
well up King Peter, on horseback, rode
out from the palace. The brilliant pro-
cesson then started for the cathedral
through the troop-lined streets. Behind the
soldiers were packed dense crowds, who, in
spite of the rainy weather, stood patiently
awaiting to see the king. The royal
heralds, cavalry and life guards {the heralds
bearing the royal standards) and carriages
with the Montenegran and Servian prin-
cesses, preceded the monarch. Beside King
Peter rode his two sons, George and Alex
ander. The cathedral was reached shortly
after O'Clock. There the representativ
of the foreign powers, the cabinet ministers
anu OlUeTS naU ALREADY Deen waiting for
some time.


AS King Peter entered the metropolitan
consecrated him and more artillery salutes
were fired The king took up his position
under a canopy and the metropolitan. as
sisted by many bishops and other clergy
commenced the solemn service, the choir
singing. Thank Thee, Our Lord After
the prayer the premier and other ministers
handed the crown and regalia to King Peter
He kissed the crown placed it on his head
and robed himself in the royal garments
An artillery salute of 101 guns then an
nounced to the people of Belgrade that
King Peter had been crowned.


Exercises Occupied Three Hours.


1t was nearly three hours before the
service was concluded and the ritual of
the church complied with. King Peter af-
terward signed the coronation document
which was witnessed by the metropolitan
the premier, the cabinet ministers and the
other heads of state. Wearing the crown
on his head and fully robed the king left
the cathedral, remounted his horse and
rode through the crowded streets to the
palace There, In the grand festal hall
Alng Peter received the congratulations of
.he diplomatic corps and others, assembled
the royal throne and once more took the
scepfer and orb in his hands. The cere-
mony or rendering homage was then per-
formed.


King Peter offered the American minister
Mr.. Jackson. the Karageorge star. which
he presented to all the other ministers as a
souvenir of the coronation. AS Mr. Jack
son was unable to accept the star. his
majesty will present him with his photo
graph and autograph.


Frantic Cheering.


The return journey from the cathedral to
the palace was marked by frantic cheering.
There had been a general fear that some
thing might happen to mar the ceremony,
and when the people saw King Peter
crowned and riding safely back their relief
found enthusiastic expression


Though all the early morning was cloudy.
when the king entered the cathedral the
sun came out, but his standards were ac-
cidentally dropped in the mud.


In the festal hall the Italian minister
greeted King Peter in the name of the triple
alliance, while the Russian minister, who
in spite of reports to the contrary, was
present, and the Roumanian and Greek
ministers handed his iesty personal let

passed before the throne and bowed to the
king, who showed no signs of fatigue.


When the king sat down on the throne
he took off the crown, which weighs four
kilos, but put 1t on again as the members
of the Skupshtna and of various corpora

though he was obliged now and again to
lift his heavy crown and rest his head

BERLIN, July 1.-The question of
mediation between Russia and Japan
on behalf of peace continues to be dis
cussed in diplomatic circles here. The
Tageblatt quotes the utterances of IN
unnamed diplomatist having close re-
lations with Japan as saying that
japan is disposed to accept the medi-
alton of some friendly power and
would propose peace conditions that
Russia could accept. Conditions could
be framed easily, since Japan does not
seek territorial acquisitions in Man
churia, but only wants the preserva-
ton of her commercial interests there
and certain influence in Korea. Hav-
ing already substantially improved her
moral position with European DOW
ers through the victories hitherto
won, Japan would gladly utilize the
situation thus created for stablishing
peace before Russia reinforces her
Manchurian army too strongly. This
diplomatist further argues that Rus
sla, after having gained one important
victory, would consent to mediation
because the war has demonstrated
that she is unable to cope with Japan
with her existing military equipment
and needs ten years for reorganization
and rearmament before renewing the
struggle. Hence the war will soon
come to an end.

TOXIC, Feb. 23.-The plan arranged
for the Emperor and the imperial head
quarters to move to Kioto has been
temporarily abandoned, and it is now
thought better not to move until after
the closing of the special session of the
Diet, early in April. The inconvenience
Of removing the seat of government
and converting the Diet in Kioto is the
reason assigned for the change in plan.


Small interest is manifested in the
forthcoming general election. The war
overshadows all political questions just
now. The country is united politically,
and it is expected that the new Diet
will fully support the Government and
cordially approve all measures concern
ing the war.


The Mikado to-day received in audi
ence Captains Lee and Paynter and
Lieutenant Boyle of the British navy
and thanked them for navigating the
japanese armored cruisers Nisshin and
Kasaga from Genoa, Italy, to Japan.
The Mikado conferred upon them, the
Order Of the Rising Sun and presented
them with gifts Of silver and lacquer
work from the imperial collection. The
foreign crew of the Nisshin will sail
for home on the steamship Siberia from
Yokohama, by way of San Francisco.

The owners cup race and class flag
regatta of the California Yacht Club
was sailed yesterday afternoon under
weather conditions that were all that
could be desired.


The Jessie E, owned by John Rosen-
field. covered herself with salt spray
and glory, winning the owners cup
and also the thirty six class flag in
two hours and three minutes. Close
behind her came the lola, owned by
Robert Vincent, and the Gypsy owned
by Charles e. Clark. All three boats
finished seconds apart. the race being
closely contested from the start.


The thirty foot-class flag was cap
tured by the Gypsy, owned and sailed
by Charles E. Clark, he having entered
his yacht in both the owners cup race.
which was open to all classes, and in
the class event.


A series of minor accidents marred
the twenty-foot class, which was won
by Harry Brindle's little salmon boat
Frolic. The other two starters, the
Anita, owned by E. Fratgo, and the
Pollywog, owned by Tyler and Bi1by.
met with mishaps which put them out
Of the race. The Pollywog lost her
rudder at the start. The Anita shipped
so much water off Mission Rock that
Tyler, who was sailing her, was forced
to give up and run for the clubhouse.


The course of the owners cup race
was from the Oakland mole, around
Alcatraz Island and Mission Rock to
the Alameda mole, twelve miles in all.
The twenty foot-class race was sailed
on the course from the Oakland mole
around Mission Rock, thence to the
Alameda mole. The water was fairly
smooth, although a stiff breeze was
blowing during all the races.

Port Arthur:


Torpedo boats Of the enemy were
discovered off Port Arthur about mid
night last night. The shore batteries
opened fire on them, but soon ceased.
At about 8 o'clock in the morning four
OF our torpedo-boats went out to sea.
Our torpedo-boats then returned.


Later two OF our torpedo boats
again went out to sea, but at once re-
turned, bringing news Of the approach
Of a japanese squadron of fourteen
ships. At about o'clock in the morn
ing this squadron opened fire at long
range"

again bombarded Port Arthur to-day
and for eight hours poured shot and
shell into the town and at the forti-
fications. The latter replied to the at

under the impression that the Cana

ly Mr.. Hill has taken one more step

breach would lose money to both
parties.

Hogue Of Valley Junction, Iowa, were
crushed to death to-day in an elevator
accident at the StatehOuse. Mrs.
HOgue was the last person to get on

the cage before she had fully got out of
reach Of the door. Her daughter, see

versed the power and the mother made
a plunge for her daughter and was
caught between the floors OF the build
ing and the roof Of the cage. Before

Guiding that it had been a case of

ture, under the care of his daughters,

NEW YORK, November 9.-Seven more
victims of the terrific gale which swept the
Atlantic coast two weeks ago were brought
here today on the steamer Trinidad from
Bermuda. The men were the survivors of
the crew of the old barkentine Elmiranda,
which was abandoned Off the Florida coast
November 10. One member of the crew,
William Mclaughlin of Weymouth, N. S.,
was swept from the deck of the water
logged craft by a gigantic wave and was
lost. The boat containing the survivors
was sighted by the British steamer Horsa
soon after the Elmiranda had been aban-
doned. and the shipwrecked sailors were
rescued and landed at Bermuda. There
they secured passage on the Trinidad,
which brought them here today.
headline: Seven More Victims of Atlantic Gale

however, I was afraid they wouldn't.

sharp. Within week more than twen-

weather and in many instances they
were unable to land passengers or
freight. Several sailers have been hur-
ried along from Newcastle, and they
all report the worst of weather. The
storm center has varied from southeast
to southwest.

The Scottish invasion of England is

reverse Of the shield is seldom seen.
The Anglicization of Scotland is going
on, silently but surely. In the matter
of Christian names the change from
Scottish to English is very significant.
correspondent, who has gone through
the invitation list of a children's ball
given this week by the Lord Provost
of Edinburgh, finds that the middle
classes in Edinburgh now give names
to their children with distinctly Eng
lish smack about them. Dorothy came
first in favor, with Gladys good sec
ond- Then followed Muriel, Ethel,
Dorys, Phyllis, Daisy. Sybil. Evelyn,
etc. Twenty years ago the middle
classes in Edinburgh adhered closely to
list which seldom included any other
names than Maggie, Jessie. Katie,
Janet. Ef1e. Annie, Nellie. Minnie, Ag-
nes, Lizzie and a few similar names.
For boys, John, Peter and Andrew are,
we are assured. being dropped, and
Highland names substituted, such as
Ronald, Ian and the like Esme, Percy
and Herbert are on the increase and
show growing appreciation of Eng
lish names among the Scottish parents.

The Minneapolis police have, had

their way to the harvest fields this
fall than in any season for years.
While thousands have passed thru the
city, few have clashed with the po-
lice. Nearly all have gone and the
Migrants now hanging around are
few.


Lats year was an uneventful one
for the harvest hands. Several were
robbed here, two were murdered al
most within the city limits and many
ran afoul of the police. Whether
there is any difference in the class
of men passing thru this year is not
known, but the police say that they
never saw a year when there was SO
little trouble.


One noticeable fact is that not
nearly so many men came to the city
this year on their way to the harvest
fields as last year. This is explained,
|perhaps, by the fact that last fall
was an Improbable one for them,
and many who went to the harvest
fields did not make a cent and are
unwilling to repeat the experiment.
The unfavorable crop reports from
the northwest, undoubtedly had some
thing to do with keeping many away.
The police expect the influx Of the
returning harvest hands about the
last of next month.

Los ANGELES, March 16.-Mrs. Sa-
die Haywood, alias Peterson. who mys-
teriously disappeared from her rooms
last Thursday and for whom the police
had been searching, fearing that her
once insane husband would murder her
returned to her mothers home this
morning. She tells a weird tale which
the police do not believe. She says that
soon after she left her home last
Thursday morning she was suddenly
seized from behind blindfolded, gagged
and thrown into a carriage. After
long ride she was taken out of the
vehicle and carried up into the third
story of a building. When the bandage
was removed from. her eyes she saw
that she was in a comfortable room,
but the windows were barred. She says
she does not know in what part of the
city this house is situated. Morning and
evening, she says, food was taken to
her room by a man or woman. This
morning about o'clock the man who
carried her away came to her room
and told her that as there had been
considerable printed about her disap-
pearance in the papers he had deter
mined to release her. Again she was
blindfolded and taken downstairs and
placed in a carriage. There was an
other long drive and then the carriage
stopped and she was put out on the
street This was at Eleventh and Geor-
gia streets.


She declares that she did not see her
husband, and that so far as she knows
he had nothing to do with her capture.
Her manner is not that of a woman who
had passed through a very narrowing
experience, and she expressed a desire
that the matter be dropped rather than
have any further investigation made.
1t is considered hardly possible that she
could have been seized on a we'll trav-
eled street in broad daylight and car
ried off without some persons witness
ing the abduction. She says she does
not know either the man or woman
who held her captive.

Another case of heroism, which happily
did not terminate fatally, occurred at Lake
Minnetonka off Orono Point yesterday aft
ernoon. Miss Anna Swenson, daughter of
Former Sheriff P. P. Swenson, was the
heroine, rescuing a drowning woman.


Miss Swenson, her sister and another
woman were in a rowboat and, as they
were nearing the shore, the boat careened.
The third woman, thinking that the boat
was going to upset, screamed and jumped
overheard. Being unable to swim, she
houndered about in the water while the
girls in the boat tried to reach her with
the one oar which had been left them.
The woman sank twice, and Miss Sven
son, seeing that they would be unable to
rescue her with the boat, sprang into the
water.


Swimming quickly to the side of the
drowning woman, she clutched her by the
dress and swan to the shore, over one
hundred feet away. Several persons who
witnessed the accident carried the unfor-
tunate woman to the Swenson residence,
where physician soon revived her. Miss
Swenson was none the worse for her duck
ing.

Billings, Mont, March 22.-Mystery
surrounds the disappearance of T. A. Will
liams. clerk of the court. While his
friends and the police have been search
ing for him for some time, no trace has
been found.

west, stopping at Helena and Portland for

there he informed his deputy that he had
collected several thousand dollars from
persons who had guaranteed payment for
scrip, and stated that he would leave that
day for Denver, and from there proceed
directly home. Nothing has been heard
from him since.

cisco yesterday says he met Williams on
the street, and that Williams, who usually
wears a beard and mustache, had had
them both shaved off, The police of both

Chicago, April 28.--The Iowa rail-

transportation to shippers Of live
stock. The members Of the commits
sion held conference here yester-

passes for the return trip. The ship
pers said that cattle were delayed in

number of claims for losses and dam
ages due to delay in transportation

Not until the commission intimated

reductions in freight rates for live

that, Ito facilitate the movement of

give free transportation to persons

roads cannot give return passes to
Iowa shippers unless they give them
also to shippers from other states.
Hence the antipass agreement will be
a dead letter hereafter.

soldiers have deserted and barracks

close to XII Jah's tomb. at o'clock In
the morning. A few shots were ex-
changed and the Russians retired.

CANTON. Ohio. September 14.-Today. the
third anniversary of the death of President
Mckinley, was noted with deep sorrow in
his home city. A wreath of flowers came
from Secretary Of Agriculture Wilson early
In the day and taken to the tomb and
laid on the casket. Other floral tributes
arrived on later trains.


Mrs Mckinley visited the tomb during
the morning to place fresh flowers on the
casket. Her condition shows little change
except that physically she is stronger. The
improved physical condition, which began
with recovery from the acute attack sus-
tanned in California and Interrupted by the
Buffalo tragedy has continued since re-
covery from the first shock and she is
now better than she had been for some
years before the Presidents death. While
she takes a deeper interest In personal and
general affairs, she seldom leaves her home
except for the drives taken almost daily.
Many old friends visit her from time to
time and she appears to find great pleasure
In their company.

text:
From the Review of Reviews


The first English walnut orchard in Cal
ifornia was planted with seed from the
Los Angeles Mission gardens, where the
padres had started a few trees with nuts
brought with them from Spain. The I'M
dertaking was success from the first, and
the acreage of walnuts has seadily in
creased-slowly at first. but now with rapid
strides. The walnut trees early age of
bearing, its long life and the steady de-
mand for it's product tend to make the en-
terprise deservedly popular. Already it Is
superseding the orange in favor among
fruit growers.


The walnut tree begins to bear when
six or seven years old. and nothing is
known definitely of it's age limit of bear
ing. Fabulous stories are told of trees in
Spain one or two centuries old, bearing
enormous crops. The oldest trees in Cali
fornia are still bearing. but deductions from
the short history already made show that
the tree is in its prime from it's twenty
fifth to its thirtieth year. Fifteen hundred
pounds of nuts TO the acre Is a good
average yield, making seventy-five pounds
the average weight from one tree


The harvest time begins about the mid
die OF September and lasts nearly six
weeks. The nuts begin to fall with the
leaves and the perfect cultivation under
the trees leaves no chance for them to lose





brown. dead leaves alone hide the nuts
Under normal conditions they drop free
from the outer husk or hull through its
irregular bursting. and getting the nuts
picked up is simple matter. Sometimes
hte trees are well irrigated just before
harvest time to insure the clean dropping of
the nuts.


Boys and girls. men and women jap
anese and Chinese. are all pressed into
service. and on hands and knees the great
orchards are gone over, not once, but sew
eral times, on account of the irregular
ripening of the nuts. The trees are occa-
sionally shaken during the season to loosen
the nuts. and before the last cleaning they
are pooled to start the very tardy ones
This is done by long, coarse, bamboo poles,
whose light weight makes them easily
handled


In certain rural districts the public
schools close regularly for a walnut vaca-
ton" The help of the children is needed.
and the children are nothing loath to re-
plenish their diminished purses. Pals.

BUTTE, Mont, Aug. 5.-A special
dispatch from Big Timber. Mont, says
a forest fire in the Crazy Mountains,
twenty miles north of Big Timber, has
done considerable damage in the last
few days. The fire started last. Sun
day, and has gradually increased until
it has burned over a large stretch OF
heavily wooded country. Parties in
town to-day from that section stated
that among the timber burned is some
of the most valuable in that district.


A dispatch from Kalispell says that
forest fires are still raging with una
bated fury in the timber lands of that
county. and from all reports received
thus far the damage will run into the
thousands of dollars. Small holders of
timber lands are the chief sufferers


The fires are not raging in the
forests surrounding this city. but in the
finest lumber sections in Northern
Montana. The thickly wooded sections
about Atlanta, Sterling and Fisher
River are burning, as we'll as the tim
ber west of Libby and between Troy
and Bonners Ferry, Idaho.


About half a dozen frame buildings
on the outskirts of White Fish have
been burned. The people living in the
timbered sections are all out fighting
the fire, but are almost powerless to
check it's advances.

CHICAGO March 25-Further details of
the damage caused by last nights storm in
the suburbs of Chicago were obtained to-
day.


At Washington Heights several persons
were injured and houses were blown down
or unroofed. In Morgan Park and Fern
wood the storm reached tornado proper
tions. Five houses were unroofed, another
blown from its foundation and miles of
telephone and telegraph poles were blown
down. Twisted telegraph wires blocked the
rock Island and Pan Handle railway
tracks. Sidewalks were wrenched from
their places. and thousands of yards of
fence scattered through the streets.


Among the injured at Washington Heights
was Mrs. 8. Scharpier, who WIS badly cut
by flying glass. The families of Peter Mel
len and Mrs. r. Ray had narrow escapes.
Mrs. Mellen and her daughters were in bed
when the storm struck. In an instant the
roof was carried away and the terrified
women were drenched by the rain.


The Ray cottage was 200 feet way. Mrs.
Ray and several friends were in the parlor
when the roof of the MelIen house crashed
upon their dwelling, wrecking the upper
story.


number of houses and stores were
badly damaged.


Traffic Suspended.


Traffic on the Calumet electric street rail-
way and the Chicago Electric Traction
Company, operating between Blue Island
and Auburn Park, was tied up for hours.


Almost every house in Burnside was dam
aged in the storm. Chimneys were blown
down, roofs torn away, and there was
scarcely an unbroken window left in the
suburb. No one was injured so far as
the police were able to learn. The water
which had flooded this portion of the city
rose about six inches In the storm.


In South Chicago the storm continued
through the night, sweeping down tele-
graph poles and flooding a part of the
town.


Fred Brunkoff of Chicago and his wife
Rebecca were severely injured when the
roof of their dwelling was blown off. Both
were struck by bricks.


Roof Hurled Against Car.


At 74th street and Railroad avenue the
wind blew the roof from building occu-
piel by Brown & Co. and hurled it against
a car on the Calumet electric line, filed
with passengers The car was knocked
from the track. None of the passengers
was injured seriously


At Dauphin Park the Illinois Central sta
tion platform and roof were torn up by
the wind and thrown across the track
stopping traffic for some time.


Many Acres Under Water.





The situation in Dauphin Park is serious
Many acres of land are under several feet
of water already, and sidewalks in the
south end of the town are submerged. Last
nights storm added materially to the grav-
ity of the situation. The total damage
there is put at $4,000.


The wind put an end to the Rogers Park
street car service in North Clark street
Between Devon and Greenleaf avenues
fallen trolley and arc light poles and tan
gled and broken wires stopped all traffic
during the night and caused the calling
of policemen and firemen to prevent fatali-
ties. Throughout Lakeview considerable
damage was done by wind and rain.


Havoc Worse Than First Believed


Reports today from the storm-swept area
in and about Chicago indicate that the
havoc wrought is even greater than at first
believed The property loss from the wind,
which was of tornado character in sew
eral districts was augmented later by
heightened floods, which had but partially
receded from previous heavy rainfalls.


In Dauphin Park and vicinity the water
has risen until the first floors of many
homes submerged, and families are
fleeing in panic by boats Business in the
town is suspended and schools are closed,
the saving of life and relief of suffering
being given the first attention.


Car Shops Center Of Storm.


The freight car shops of the Nickel Plate
railroad were the center of a miniature tor
nado. The large building used repair
shop was partly wrecked, the roof being
hurled against adjoining building. About
the shops were large number of freight
cars. Many of these were thrown from the
tracks, while others were unroofed.

thirty-six hours of steady work the re-

telephone companies when the serious

succeeded in patching up the main lines,

ed under most discouraging conditions

circuits were still In use. Wall street was
in much better condition than yesterday.

Union, and there were two wires between
New York and the cattle and grain mar
kets in Chicago. The Chicago wires were
working slowly, however and were hours
behind in handling the regular routine
business.

telegraph and telephone poles were blown
down during the storm, the wires were
still out of service

The last source of gutta percha developed
is that in the Philippine Islands, but here
the regions which produce this material for
the market are confined to the islands of
Mindanao and Tawi-Tawi. The method of
harvesting used at present by the natives
consists in cutting down the large trees,
ringing the trunk, Topping off the larger
branches and then catching the milk as it
flows out. This is very wasteful, as but a
small part of the milk is secured. For
tunately. however, this process pays only
with large trees, so that the smaller ones
are not destroyed. This method of harvest
ing has been prohibited and rules provided
for tapping the trees. but these have never
been enforced. At the present time the
gutta percha trees have disappeared from
the coast regions and are along the large
rivers.


The various governments with tropical
possessions In the east are studying the
gntta percha and rubber situation, with q
view of determining proper methods of
propagation and harvesting.

A dispatch from Chicago says: An alarm
clock gave the signal for Cora Galloway, a
Waukegan girl, twenty years old, to jump
into the lake in an effort to end life Of
misery.


The girl had set the alarm for the exact
moment at which she thought Allen jack
son, whom she loved, was to marry an
other.


Taking the clock with her. she walked
on to the pier and waited. She had writ
ten a farewell note to her sister. and was
prepared to die. Finally the alarm sound
ed and the young woman leaped into the
water Her skirts buoyed her up and her
attempts to get her head under the water
were vain. Her splashing was heard by
two men who procured boat and rescued
her, despite her resistance.


After Miss Galloway was taken from
the water she learned that her alarm
clock was two weeks behind time, for her
sweetheart was married a fortnight ago.

LONDON, Feb. ia correspondent
who says he was an eyewitness of the
Port Arthur naval fight sends from
YinkOw (Manchuria), the port of New
chwang, under date Of February IL, the
following uncensored story:


About midnight on Monday the town
was aroused by the firing of big guns.
Six Japanese torpedo boats had ap-
preached within half mile of the Rus
sian fleet and were showing lights,
tunnels and signals just like those of
the Russians. The Japanese torpedo
beats crept quite close to the Russian
ships before they were discovered.
Each of the Japanese boats discharged
torpedoes, three of which took effect,
striking the battleships Cesarevitch and
Retz1van and the cruiser Pallada- The
three damaged ships returned to the
harbor to avoid sinking.


notwithstanding the continuous fire
from the ships and forts four of the
Japanese torpedo boats escaped. One,
however, was sunk and another, which
was in sinking condition, was desert
ed by the crew and was afterward cap
tured by the Russians. The action
ceased at o'clock in the morning


The loss on the Russian ships was
eight killed and twenty wounded.


Apart from the disablement of three
Russian ships the damage done to the
fleet and forts was not very great.


The Japanese fleet again came in
sight about IL o'clock on Tuesday fore
noon. There were in all fifteen ships in
two lines of battle-six battleships, six
first-class cruisers and three second
class cruisers. The Russians had out
side thirteen large vessels under Ad-
miral Stark. After the commencement
of the action the populace fled toward
the hill outside of town.


On both sides 1 counted more than
300 shells, few Of which reached the
mark. The others did not explode.


The Japanese warships steamed slow
ly past, in line of battle, to the west
ward and about four miles off. each
vessel beginning to fire when opposite
the Russian ships, which were two
miles off shore. The action became gen.
eral. There was no maneuvering, sim
ply heavy and fast firing.


The firing ceased at noon, the jap
anese ships withdrawing to the south
ward, having one battleship and one
large cruiser put out of action. One
small boat was chased and was sunk
by the Novik (Russian), which after
ward received a shell at the water line,
but reached port all right. Admiral
Stark signaling well DONE" while all
the rest of the fleet cheered her ar
rival. Even the three Russian ships
aground fired during the action.


The casualties on the Russian side
were twenty-five killed and sixty-fou
wounded. Nearly half of the casual
ties occurred on the Pallada and Novik.


The Japanese fleet sailed southwark
at p. m. and all was quiet.

cially due to Gen. Kondratenko, Col. Ir1nan.

troops manifest heroic spirit. Wounded
men are daily returning to the ranks from
the hospitals. We pray to God for victory,
and for the health Of your Majesty"

states that between Sept. 10 and Sept. 20
the Japanese captured two redoubts near
the aqueduct, but all their other assaults
were repulsed. He adds that when the

stranded schooner McClelland.

schooner. The lifeboat was demolished, the men
saving their lives by jumping and catching the
low ratings OF the schooner.

beach, launched their boat and forced her

direction of Naval Constructor Baxter and
his aid, Assistant Constructor Robinson
went through series of maneuvers cover
ing the mechanical part of the launching
ceremony.


Final Rehearsal Completed.

Alice Welles, the Connecticut girl who will
name the battle ship, was in attendance. The
grease-coyered ways along which the Con-
necticut will glide into the water have been
covered with canvas lest sand or dust get
into the grease layer and make friction
which might set fire to the wooden cradle
in which the big ship rests the moment her
tourney toward the river begins. The men,
who unfasten the wooden props that hold
the vessel captive work in three relays.
To each relay are assigned the work of
knocking loose one set of the wooden beams
with which the ship Is held.

South Norwalk, Conn, Jan. 14.-William Car
penter, twenty-one years old. shot and seriously
wounded his sweetheart, Miss Margaret Nevils,
tonight. Carpenter fired at the girl three times.
and each shot took effect. Miss Nevils car
ried to the South Norwalk Hospital, and the
physicians. after examination. said that the
girls condition was critical Carpenter at
tempted to escape after the shooting, but was
caught by the police. At Police Headquarters
he confessed to Chief Vollmer. but said that the
shooting was not premeditated.


Carpenter, whose home is In Stamford, has
been calling Miss Nevils for some time. To-
night he had argument with the girls
mother When he left the house Miss Nevils
accompanied him to the street. where. accord
ing TO his own story. he renewed the argument
with the girl, who had been unfolding her
mother. The couple were walking near the
Nevis home. when Carpenter suddenly drew
a revolver from his pocket and fired three shots
in rapid succession at the girl One bullet en-
tered one of the girls lungs. another struck her
in the chin and the third made a giancing
wound on the cheek. The first bullet was the
most serious of the three and at the hospital II
was feared that it had penetrated the abdominal
wall and entered the stomach.


Carpenter, after firing the shots turned and
ran across a vacant lot and out onto the street
He had just started down the street when he
into the arms of a policeman who had heard
the shots and who was hurrying to investigate
the cause The policeman took Carpenter TO the
hospital to which Miss Nevils had been re-
moved.


The young woman identified Carpenter as the
man who fired the shots Carpenter was then
taken TO the police station, where he broke
down and cried violently. He admitted the
shooting, but said that in the heat OF an argu-
ment with the girl he lost his head and fred
the shots without realizing what he was doing

A double truckload of curious and rare carvings
yesterday represented the largest seizure OF SNUG
gled goods made for many months In this port
They came from the steamer Indrawadi. consigned
to Funch. Edge & Co.. from Kobe, Mol, Shanghai.
Manila, Singapore. Suez and Port Said


The Customs officials have been watching the
steamers from these ports for some time, it hav-
ing to their knowledge that smuggling on
large scale was going on Yesterday when the
manifest of the Indrawadi was sent to the Collector
OF the Port it sent back to Captain Cullington
with request that he look over 1T and see II
there were any omissions. Captain Cullington said
that his entire cargo had been entered on the
manifest.


Treasury Agents Cooley and O'Neill then visited
the steamer, and told Captain CullingtOn that de-
spite his assertion that everything had been duly
entered the manifest they would search the
entire vessel The two agents first sounded all me
deck plankings, and wherever there was a sus
picious sound ripped up the boards being rewarded
by the discovery of several caches. They then
entered the hold and made a thorough search
Forward they found bulkhead that had no APP
parent excuse for existing. Sledges requis-
toned from the carpenter and the bulkhead
smashed In. Stored behind 1t they found chest
after chest full of costly carvings and Oriental
curios Then returning the tools to the carpenters
room. Cooley thought to pry open suspiciously
heavily iron bound and strongly locked carpenters
chest. On top the usual assortment of chisels
and files but when this tray lifted the officers
found the remainder of the chest full OF carved
ivory, wooden and jade ornaments.


Forty-two cases of Oriental curios, three sets Of
silk and ebony screens four boxes of ostrich and
peacock plumes. several boxes of the finest quality
of china tea services, hundreds of silk handker-
chiefs found in and concealed In the sailors
hunks. several lots of Satsuma vases and hundreds
of small carved ivory and wooden figures, were
seized. The screens confscated stand four
feet high, and have carved ebony frames backed
with the heaviest china silk deliberately embroid-
cred with dragons. butterflies and other Oriental
designs.


The carvings found in the carpenters chest. 1t IS
believed, formed part OF the loot taken from the
Winter Palace at Picking by the soldiers OF the
allied powers. When the customs officials sought
to find an owner for the goods. they unsuc-
cessfu- The captain was mucn surprised to think
they could have got aboard without his knowI-
edge. and so were the crew and the other officers.
When the two Treasury agents first went on
board the Indrawadi they saw half a dozen deal
ers in Oriental goods on the wharf. The value Of
the seized goods is estimated 10 be over 5000 No
arrests were made

The dried and evaporated fruits that
come from California are most excellent
and inexpensive. The apricots, with their
suggestion of just the right degree of tart
ness are delicious. and the only reason
they are not more widely known is that
the average cook does not know how to
prepare them, and the result is libel on
the fruit. They require careful washing,
piece by piece, between the thumb and fore
finger, long soaking over night for twelve
or fourteen hours. and then gentle SIM
mering In the water in which they We're
soaked until fresh and tender. Very little
sugar is required, and tbs should be added
about twenty minutes before taking from
the fire Prunes are at their best when,
after the preliminary soaking, they are
cooked in an old-fashioned pipkin in the
oven for three four hours. If the water
cooks away, add more. Many good cooks
add no sugar at all to prunes cooked In
this way, the long cooking bringing out all
the sweetness of the fruit. Peaches end
plums cooked in this way become rich
conserve embedded in liquid that is almost
a jelly


Apples require longer .oakfng, but shorter
cooking. If the choicest evaporated fruit
is used there will be scant difference be-
tween the apple sauce" made from the
fresh apples and that from the evaporataa,
save in the price, the evaporated apples IN
most places being much the cheaper.

The schooner Webfoot. dismasted
and waterlogged. which was towed
into Astoria Wednesday night by the
tug Wallula, is one Of the oldest and
best known vessels in the coasting
trade She was built in 1869 at Coos
Bay and for thirty-fve years has been
in active commission. She was built
for and is still owned by the Simpson
Lumber Company Formerly a bark
entine, she was converted some time
ago into a three-masted schooner. Her
career has been remarkably free from
mishap and since she slid from her
cradle at the Oregon seaport she has
earned much money for her owners.


The Webfoot was bound from Coos
Bay for this port. She encountered
heavy gales and November Is became
waterlogged. Three days later the
masts carried away and when picked
up by the steamer George w. Elder
Captain Lewis and his men had about
abandoned hope The tug Wallula re-
lieved the Elder of her tow and the
Webfoot is now safe in Astoria.


Three CT the crew, who left the boat
to seek assistance, are still missing
and little hope is entertained at As
toria for their safety.


At the time the men left the vessel
great seas were running and shipping
men are certain that the small boat
succumbed to the fury or the elements.
The men had been without food for
four days and also without water, and
unquestionably viii have perished
from hunger by this time if the ocean
has not claimed them as victims. Mate
Bromer, Seaman ]. O'Neil and another
sailor whose name is unknown COM
prised the party who started off on the
fCrlorn expedition. There is a bare
possibility that they managed TO
weather the seas and that a passing
steamer may have picked them up and
taken them to Puget Sound or to San
Francisco, but no one here doubts that
they have either starved to death or
been drowned

NEW YORK, March 19.-Three
Standard Oil Company tugs, two fire
boats and the entire fire department of
Elizabeth, n. j.. were called out early
this morning to prevent the spread of
an oil fire which caused loss estimated
at 100000 and which threatened with
destruction the extensive oil works of
the Borne & Scrymser Company at
E.lizabethport, n. j., and neighboring
plants and lumber yards.


The plant was partly destroyed on
the night OF February 81, causing a loss
of s75,000 The second fire began at
nearly the same hour from the
same cause-spontaneous combustion.
Spreading into the main plant. which
consists of eight or ten buildings and a
dozen big oil tanks. the fire became so
hot that the firemen could only bend
their efforts toward keeping it within
bounds.


Two oil tanks exploded, spreading
their blazing contents in all directions.
Fortunately the wind was blowing
from the northwest, carrying the flames
and ignited oil into Staten Island
Sound. Two schooners were taken out
into the sound to escape the burning
oil that drifted across the water Rivers
of burning oil began flowing after the
explosion in all directions across the
property of the company, which fronts
on the waters edge. A change of wind
would have carried the fire directly
into Elizabethport and probably caused
great loss.

out the states of Wisconsin, Illinois, Mis-
souri,, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota and the
northwestern part of Indiana.

BELGRADE, Servia, Sept. 21.-
Peter Karageorgevitch was crowned
, King of Servia to-day. There were no
hostile demonstrations and no attempt
to carry out the numerous threats
against the new Kings life.


Here and in every garrison town Of
Servia the dawn of the day was
marked by a salute of twenty-one guns
and before the sun was we'll up King
Peter, on horseback, rode out from the
palace. The procession then started
for the Cathedral through the troop
lined streets. The royal heralds,
cavalry and life guards (the heralds
bearing the royal standards) and car
riages with the Montenegran and Ser
Wan Princesses preceded the monarch.
Beside King Peter rode his two sons,
George and Alexander.


AS King Peter entered the Cathedral
the Metropolitan consecrated him and
more artillery salutes were fired. The
King then took up his position under
a canopy and the Metropolitan, assist
ed by many Bishops and other clergy,
commenced the solemn service, the
choir singing Thank Thee, Our Lord"
After the prayer the Premier and
other Ministers handed the crown and
regalia to King Peter. He kissed the
crown, placed it on his head and robed
himself in the royal garments. An ar
tillery salute of 101 guns then an
nounced to the people of Belgrade that
King Peter had been crowned.


Wearing the crown on his head and
fully robed the King left the Cathe-
dral, remounted his horse and rode
through the crowded streets to the
palace. There, in the grand festal hall.
King Peter received the congratula-
tions of the diplomatic corps and
others, ascended the royal throne and
once more took the sceptre and orb
in his hands. The ceremony of rem
derlng homage was then performed.
